correctness.rationale: For a genuine supporting-base pyramid K=conv(F∪{a}), every extreme point besides a lies in F and the apex is unique. Distinct cone directions have distinct apexes because the base is the closed convex hull of all extreme points except the apex. For k directions, affine functionals ell_i vanish on respective bases, are positive at a_i and vanish at all other apexes; these imply the apices are affinely independent, k<=n+1. If k=n+1, all other extreme points would lie in the empty intersection of the simplex facet hyperplanes, forcing K to be that simplex. If k<=n, full-dimensionality gives another extreme point b lying in every H_i; translating the functionals to b makes their linear normals independent, so the common affine intersection L has dimension n-k. With B=K∩L, Krein–Milman (finite-dimensional) gives K=conv(B∪{a_i}) and full-dimensionality forces dim B=n-k. For k=n or n-1 this makes B a point or segment and K a simplex, contradicting k<n+1. Conversely simplices have n+1 apex directions. For every 0<=k<=n-2, pyramid over an m=n-k>=2 cross-polytope has exactly k cone apexes: deleting any ±e_j leaves a set affinely spanning the base m-space, so no cross-polytope vertex is an apex. Separately coded exact SymPy rank checks verified every k for 2<=n<=10 (54 cases), corroborating witness arithmetic only, not providing the universal proof.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: One cone direction corresponds to one apex with all other extreme points on a base facet; for a polytope this is a loop in the facet-complement incidence hypergraph. Feldman uses the identical object and proves finiteness only; Werner–Wotzlaw treats the stronger global hypothesis that each facet has at most two vertices outside and classifies special polytope joins. value.rationale: The theorem settles the specific n+1 simplex-only cone-direction question posed immediately after Feldman’s 2026 finiteness lemma. It strengthens that bound to the full dimension-by-dimension set of possible counts, excludes n and n−1 outside simplices and canonically identifies the residual base of every nonsimplex cone in arbitrary full-dimensional convex bodies, including nonpolytopal ones. These are motivated precise structural facts not arbitrary finite slices or a mere numerical test. The proof uses elementary affine geometry, but the explicit recently stated question and additional decomposition give it independent mathematical significance.
